andragogy.courses.title: CS201 Data Structures — project-based track
andragogy.courses.description: A project-first route through Data Structures for B.Tech CSE Semester 3. Every module starts from a product you would actually build — a music playlist, a calculator, a campus shuttle router — and the data structure is learned because the product needs it.

principles.needToKnow: Each module opens with the engineering problem and the placement-interview question it answers (e.g. 'why does Spotify's queue use a doubly linked list?'). Learners see the mid-sem outcome they are working on and their current mastery.
principles.selfConcept: Learners choose the order of the elective modules (Hashing case, Sorting benchmark lab), pick their own project dataset and set personal goals that the faculty mentor reviews — not grades.
principles.experience: Week-1 profile captures prior coding (competitive programming, internships, hackathons). Experienced coders are invited to pair with first-time programmers; reflections ask learners to connect each structure to apps they already use.
principles.readiness: Sequenced to land before the November placement-prep drive and the end-semester exam; trees and graphs are timed after the Mid-Semester Test so feedback is fresh.
principles.orientation: Modules are organised around problems (route a shuttle, evaluate an expression, index student records) rather than chapters. Deliverables are working GitHub repositories with test cases.
principles.motivation: Showcase demo day with alumni from product companies, GitHub portfolio credit and peer-tutor recognition for learners who master a module early.

reviewHistory.note: Excellent alignment with mid-sem outcomes. Please keep the demo day.

andragogy.courses.title: CS203 DBMS — case method
andragogy.courses.description: Database design taught the way practising engineers meet it: through real Indian systems — a hospital OPD, a railway booking platform, a UPI-scale ledger. Learners analyse each case, defend a design and then build it.

principles.needToKnow: Each case begins with a production incident (double-booked berth, slow OPD queue report) so learners see the cost of poor schema design before learning the theory.
principles.selfConcept: Learners take and defend a position in case discussions; the transactions case is an elective that learners can schedule when ready.
principles.experience: Learners who have built college fest or hackathon apps share their schemas as live examples in the ER modelling discussion.
principles.readiness: Aligned with the SQL round of internship interviews scheduled in November.
principles.orientation: Every module is a case with a decision to make — not a chapter to cover.

andragogy.courses.title: MA201 Discrete Mathematics — puzzle studio
andragogy.courses.description: Proof and counting skills learned through puzzles from competitive programming and system design — pigeonhole in hashing, induction in recursion, graph theory in networks.

principles.needToKnow: Each puzzle is tied to a coding-interview pattern so learners see why proofs matter for programmers.
principles.selfConcept: Learners pick 3 of 5 puzzle sets and choose to work solo or in pairs.
principles.readiness: Runs alongside CS201 graphs so graph theory is immediately applicable.
principles.orientation: Problem-centred: every session starts with a puzzle, not a definition.
principles.motivation: Weekly puzzle leaderboard (opt-in) and a 'proof of the week' wall.

reviewHistory.note: Ready for review before the Nov start.

andragogy.courses.title: PD101 Teaching for competency-based education
andragogy.courses.description: A practice-based professional development course for Greenfield teachers preparing for CBSE's shift to competency-based assessment. Teachers bring their own question papers, answer scripts and lesson plans and redesign them during the course.

principles.needToKnow: CBSE's 2026-27 assessment scheme sets 50% competency-based questions in Class 10 board papers. Each module shows teachers the gap between their current papers and the CBSE sample paper.
principles.selfConcept: Teachers set their own PD goals, choose electives (Differentiation, Feedback Clinic) and decide which of their own classes to try ideas in.
principles.experience: Built on teachers' own artefacts: last term's Periodic Test papers, real (anonymised) answer scripts and their lesson plans are the course material.
principles.readiness: Timed before the Half-Yearly Examination paper-setting window so new skills are used immediately.
principles.orientation: Every module produces something teachers need this term — a redesigned question set, a marking scheme, a differentiated lesson.
principles.motivation: Recognised in the annual appraisal, shared in the staff-room 'best practice' showcase, and linked to each teacher's professional improvement plan.

reviewHistory.note: Approved. Let us align the timeline with the Half-Yearly paper-setting.

andragogy.courses.title: PD102 Using assessment data to plan remediation
andragogy.courses.description: A short follow-on course: teachers read outcome-level results from the Periodic Tests and plan targeted remediation for their own sections.

principles.needToKnow: Teachers see their own class's outcome heatmap from Periodic Test 2 and the outcomes where most students need support.
principles.selfConcept: Each teacher chooses which section and which two outcomes to remediate.
principles.experience: Starts from what remediation strategies teachers already use and which ones worked.
principles.readiness: Runs in the two weeks after Periodic Test 2 results are published.
principles.orientation: The problem is real: a group of learners in your class who are below 40% on an outcome.

andragogy.courses.title: Data analytics foundations — self-paced
andragogy.courses.description: A self-directed path from spreadsheets to data storytelling, designed around Arjun's goal of moving from sales operations into an analyst role. Each module uses his own (anonymised) sales MIS data.

principles.needToKnow: Every module maps to a task in analyst job descriptions on Naukri and LinkedIn for Mumbai-based roles.
principles.selfConcept: Fully self-paced; the learner sets weekly hours and chooses whether to do the storytelling elective before or after visualisation.
principles.experience: Five years of sales operations experience: modules reuse the weekly MIS reports already built in Excel.
principles.readiness: Prepared for the internal analyst opening expected in Q1 2027.
principles.orientation: Each module ends in a work-ready artefact (cleaned dataset, SQL report, dashboard, story deck).
principles.motivation: Career growth and the satisfaction of automating a 4-hour weekly report.

andragogy.courses.title: MBA-101 Managerial Economics (Online MBA · CDOE)
andragogy.courses.description: Economic reasoning for working managers in the online MBA run by the Centre for Distance and Online Education. Each module starts from a decision a Lucknow business actually faces (pricing a festive box, sizing a cloud kitchen, launching a chikankari line online) and brings in the theory that decision needs.

delivery.note: Video lectures, unit quizzes and the proctored final test run on Walnut LMS. Live sessions are on Saturday evenings. Importing Walnut LMS results into the Learning Suite is a planned integration.

principles.needToKnow: Each module opens with the business decision it helps with and the course outcomes it builds. Learners see their latest unit-quiz and final-test evidence for those outcomes before they start.
principles.selfConcept: Most learners work full time. They choose when to study each module during the week, pick the business they analyse in assignments (often their own employer or family business) and decide whether to take the Union Budget elective.
principles.experience: The week-1 profile records each learner's work experience. Live sessions pair learners from sales, operations and finance, and reflections ask them to connect each idea to a decision from their own job.
principles.readiness: Sequenced around the work calendar: the demand and pricing modules land before the festive season, and the Union Budget elective runs in February when the Budget is presented.
principles.orientation: Modules are organised around problems (price this product, forecast that demand, find the break-even point) rather than chapters. Deliverables are short memos a manager could send to a director.
principles.motivation: Learners who master a unit early are invited to tutor peers, and strong assignment memos are shared with the CDOE alumni network as examples.

reviewHistory.note: Ready for the August intake. Online content is on Walnut LMS.
Approved for the 2026-27 online MBA. Please keep the live sessions on Saturdays for working learners.

andragogy.courses.title: BCM-301 Corporate Accounting
andragogy.courses.description: Company accounts for B.Com Semester 3, taught in the classroom through practice problems drawn from realistic (fictional) Lucknow companies: a start-up's share issue, a textile amalgamation, a handloom company's Schedule III accounts.

delivery.note: Classroom teaching in the Department of Commerce, with tutorials on Thursdays.

principles.needToKnow: Every module starts with the document a commerce graduate will be handed at work (a prospectus, a trial balance, a scheme of amalgamation) and the outcomes the sessional tests check.
principles.selfConcept: Students choose their practice set level, set their own goals for the sessional tests and decide when to attempt the optional holding-company module.
principles.experience: Several students help with family businesses or do articleship preparation. Reflections ask them to connect journal entries to the accounts they have seen at home or at work.
principles.readiness: Final accounts are timed just before the end-semester examination and the CA Intermediate registration window, when students most want them.
principles.orientation: Problem-centred: each class starts with a short case and a decision, not with a definition.
principles.motivation: Students who master a unit early become peer tutors for the batch, which counts towards the department's academic recognition certificate.

reviewHistory.note: Approved. Good use of local company examples.

andragogy.modules.title: Playlist manager with linked lists
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: Music apps like JioSaavn let you add, remove and drag songs around a queue thousands of times a day. Arrays make reordering expensive; linked lists make it cheap. You will build the queue that sits behind 'Play next'.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A C/Java playlist manager (insert, delete, move-up/down, shuffle) with unit tests and a one-page complexity comparison vs an array implementation.

phases.name: Meet the problem
phases.activity: Watch a 3-minute screen recording of a playlist being reordered. In teams of 3, list every operation the app performs and guess its cost.

phases.name: Identify learning gaps
phases.activity: Team KWL board: what do we know about arrays, what do we need to know about pointers and nodes? Each learner writes one personal learning question.

phases.name: Self-directed study
phases.activity: Self-study the curated resources; implement singly linked insert/delete before attempting doubly linked move operations.

phases.name: Apply & solve
phases.activity: Build the playlist manager, run the shared test-suite and benchmark 10,000 random operations against an ArrayList version.

phases.name: Reflect
phases.activity: Team retrospective: which design decision would you change? Individual journal entry on how your understanding of pointers changed.

andragogy.modules.title: Stacks at work: build an expression evaluator
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: Every calculator app, spreadsheet formula bar and compiler front-end converts infix expressions with a stack. You will build the engine behind a GST calculator that handles brackets and operator precedence.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: An infix-to-postfix converter and evaluator that passes 25 test expressions, plus a deque-based undo/redo extension.

phases.name: Before class
phases.activity: Watch the stack primer and complete the infix-to-postfix tracing worksheet (first 10 expressions). Note one question for class.

phases.name: In class
phases.activity: Peer instruction: trace tricky expressions in pairs, then implement the evaluator live with the faculty reviewing edge cases (unary minus, nested brackets).

phases.name: After class
phases.activity: Extend your evaluator with undo/redo using a deque and write a short reflection on when a queue would have been the wrong choice.

andragogy.modules.title: BST and AVL: indexing student records
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: The college ERP looks up 6,000 student records by roll number every morning for attendance. A sorted array is slow to update; an unbalanced tree degrades badly. You will feel this before you fix it.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A BST and an AVL tree indexing 10,000 roll numbers, with a timing chart showing why balancing matters for sequential inserts.

phases.name: Concrete experience
phases.activity: Insert roll numbers CSE3-001 to CSE3-500 in order into the naive BST provided and time 1,000 lookups. Then shuffle and repeat.

phases.name: Reflective observation
phases.activity: Journal: why did sequential inserts behave so differently from shuffled ones? Sketch the tree shape you think you created.

phases.name: Abstract conceptualisation
phases.activity: Study BST deletion cases and AVL rotations using the visualiser and case study. Derive the height bound in your own words.

phases.name: Active experimentation
phases.activity: Implement AVL insertion with rotations, re-run the timing experiment and present the before/after chart to your team.

andragogy.modules.title: Graph routing: campus shuttle planner
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: Horizon's 14 hostel and academic blocks are served by two shuttles. Students wait up to 25 minutes. Model the campus as a weighted graph and propose routes that cut the average wait.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A shuttle-routing tool using BFS/DFS for connectivity and Dijkstra for shortest paths, with a 5-minute pitch to the transport committee.

phases.name: Meet the problem
phases.activity: Walk-through of the campus map and the transport office's complaint log. Teams restate the problem in their own words.

phases.name: Identify learning gaps
phases.activity: Identify what you need to learn: graph representations, traversal, shortest path. Each learner picks one area to research and teach back.

phases.name: Self-directed study
phases.activity: Use the traversal visualiser; implement adjacency lists, BFS and DFS; then study Dijkstra with a priority queue.

phases.name: Apply & solve
phases.activity: Build the planner on the real campus graph, compare at least two routing options and present recommendations.

phases.name: Reflect
phases.activity: Debrief: what did the problem teach you that a textbook exercise would not? Peer feedback on team process.

andragogy.modules.title: Hashing design case: UPI transaction lookup
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: A payments start-up must confirm whether a UPI transaction ID has already been processed in under 5 ms, across 40 million transactions a day. Their first hash table is suffering from collisions.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A 2-page design memo recommending a collision-resolution strategy and load factor, backed by a small benchmark.

phases.name: Pre-read the case
phases.activity: Read the case 'PaySetu's Duplicate Payment Problem' (provided by faculty) and the incident timeline.

phases.name: Individual analysis
phases.activity: Individually decide: chaining, open addressing or cuckoo hashing? Write a 150-word position with one number to support it.

phases.name: Group discussion
phases.activity: Facilitated debate in two camps; the faculty plays the CTO pushing back on memory cost.

phases.name: Synthesis
phases.activity: Synthesise design principles for hash tables at scale and map them to Java's HashMap implementation.

andragogy.modules.title: Sorting benchmark lab
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: An e-commerce seller dashboard sorts 2 lakh orders by date, amount and pincode. Which sort is stable, which is fastest, and does it matter?
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A benchmark notebook comparing 4 sorting algorithms on real-shaped data, with a recommendation for each column type.

phases.name: Concrete experience
phases.activity: Run the provided sorting implementations on the orders dataset and record timings.

phases.name: Reflective observation
phases.activity: Reflect on surprises — why did insertion sort win on nearly-sorted data?

phases.name: Abstract conceptualisation
phases.activity: Formalise complexity, stability and binary search variants.

phases.name: Active experimentation
phases.activity: Choose and justify a sort for each dashboard column; implement lower-bound search for pincode filters.

andragogy.modules.title: Case: designing the OPD database for City Hospital
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: A 300-bed hospital in Bengaluru still runs its outpatient department on registers. Patients wait 90 minutes. Design the data model for a token-based OPD system.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: An ER diagram with cardinalities and a 1-page justification of key design choices.

phases.name: Pre-read the case
phases.activity: Pre-read the City Hospital case and the OPD process map.

phases.name: Individual analysis
phases.activity: Draft your own ER model and list three assumptions.

phases.name: Group discussion
phases.activity: Compare models in groups; defend how you modelled doctors, slots and follow-ups.

phases.name: Synthesis
phases.activity: Extract ER modelling principles you would reuse in any booking system.

andragogy.modules.title: SQL detective: investigate with joins
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: A fraud analyst at a bank must find suspicious account patterns using SQL only. Speed matters — queries must run on 5 million rows.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A set of 10 investigative queries with EXPLAIN plans before and after adding indexes.

phases.name: Meet the problem
phases.activity: Receive the case file: three suspicious transactions and a database dump.

phases.name: Identify learning gaps
phases.activity: List the SQL skills you need: joins, GROUP BY, subqueries, indexes.

phases.name: Self-directed study
phases.activity: Work through SQL Detective and the indexing notes at your own pace.

phases.name: Apply & solve
phases.activity: Solve the case and optimise your two slowest queries.

phases.name: Reflect
phases.activity: Reflect on how you debugged wrong results.

andragogy.modules.title: Case: normalising a railway booking system
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: A legacy booking table with 48 columns causes update anomalies every Tatkal morning. Normalise it without breaking reports.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A normalised schema up to BCNF with functional dependency analysis.

phases.name: Pre-read the case
phases.activity: Read the booking-table case and the anomaly reports.

phases.name: Individual analysis
phases.activity: Identify functional dependencies individually.

phases.name: Group discussion
phases.activity: Debate: is BCNF worth it here, or is 3NF enough?

phases.name: Synthesis
phases.activity: Synthesise a normalisation checklist.

andragogy.modules.title: Case: the double-booked berth (transactions)
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: Two passengers were confirmed on the same berth during a Tatkal rush. Find the concurrency bug.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: An incident post-mortem explaining the anomaly and the isolation level that prevents it.

phases.name: Pre-read the case
phases.activity: Read the incident timeline and server logs.

phases.name: Individual analysis
phases.activity: Identify which ACID property was violated.

phases.name: Group discussion
phases.activity: Group discussion on isolation levels and their performance cost.

phases.name: Synthesis
phases.activity: Write transferable rules for designing concurrent booking systems.

andragogy.modules.title: Induction through recursion puzzles
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: Recursive functions in interviews are proofs by induction in disguise.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: Three induction proofs for recursive functions you have written.

phases.name: Concrete experience
phases.activity: Solve the Tower of Hanoi puzzle for n = 1..5 and count moves.

phases.name: Reflective observation
phases.activity: Reflect: what pattern did you notice and how sure are you it always holds?

phases.name: Abstract conceptualisation
phases.activity: Learn the structure of induction proofs.

phases.name: Active experimentation
phases.activity: Prove the move count formula and two recursion properties of your own code.

andragogy.modules.title: Pigeonhole and counting in hashing
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: Why must every hash function have collisions? Counting arguments answer system design questions.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A worked counting argument for collision guarantees in a hash table design.

andragogy.modules.title: From recall to competency: rewriting board questions
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: Last term's Periodic Test 2 paper for Class 10 had 78% recall-type questions. The CBSE 2026-27 sample paper has 50% competency-based questions. Your students will meet the board pattern in March.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: Five of your own recall questions rewritten as competency-based questions (case-based, source-based or assertion–reason), with the outcome each assesses.

phases.name: Pre-read the case
phases.activity: Read the case 'Two papers, one syllabus' comparing a Greenfield PT-2 paper with the CBSE sample paper. Bring your own last paper.

phases.name: Individual analysis
phases.activity: Classify each question in your paper by Bloom's level and question type; mark three you would change.

phases.name: Group discussion
phases.activity: Department discussion: what makes a question 'competency-based' and not just long? Rewrite one question together.

phases.name: Synthesis
phases.activity: Synthesise a checklist for competency-based questions and rewrite five of your own.

andragogy.modules.title: Step-wise marking schemes that reward method
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: Re-evaluation requests in Class 10 Maths rose last year because method marks were applied inconsistently. A clear step-wise scheme protects students and teachers.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A step-wise marking scheme for one 5-mark question, moderated by a colleague, plus three sample scripts marked against it.

phases.name: Concrete experience
phases.activity: Mark three anonymised answer scripts for the same question without a scheme. Compare your marks with a colleague's.

phases.name: Reflective observation
phases.activity: Reflect: where did your marks differ and why? What did you reward — method, answer or presentation?

phases.name: Abstract conceptualisation
phases.activity: Study CBSE's step-wise marking principles and the sample schemes for maths and science.

phases.name: Active experimentation
phases.activity: Write a scheme for your own question, re-mark the scripts and check whether agreement improved.

andragogy.modules.title: Questioning across Bloom's levels
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: Classroom observations at Greenfield found 84% of teacher questions were at the 'Remember' level. Higher-order questioning drives the competencies the board now tests.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A questioning plan for one lesson with at least two questions at each of Apply, Analyse and Evaluate, tried in class.

phases.name: Before class
phases.activity: Watch the annotated model lesson and tag each teacher question with its Bloom's level.

phases.name: In class
phases.activity: Micro-teaching in the staff room: deliver a 7-minute segment while a colleague logs question levels.

phases.name: After class
phases.activity: Use the plan in one of your sections and journal what changed in student responses.

andragogy.modules.title: Differentiating for support and stretch
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: In most Class 10 sections, the gap between the top and bottom quartile on Periodic Test 2 is over 50 percentage points. One lesson plan rarely serves both.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: One of your lesson plans adapted with a support track and a stretch track, tried with a real section.

phases.name: Meet the problem
phases.activity: Look at your section's PT-2 spread and pick a lesson where the gap hurts most.

phases.name: Identify learning gaps
phases.activity: List what you need: grouping strategies, tiered tasks, scaffolds.

phases.name: Self-directed study
phases.activity: Self-study differentiation strategies and a colleague's example.

phases.name: Apply & solve
phases.activity: Redesign the lesson and try it.

phases.name: Reflect
phases.activity: Reflect with a peer on what worked for each group.

andragogy.modules.title: Feedback clinic: outcome-linked comments
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: 'Good', 'Revise' and 'Be careful' are the three most common comments on Greenfield answer scripts. Students cannot act on them.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: Ten comments from your own scripts rewritten as actionable, outcome-linked feedback.

phases.name: Concrete experience
phases.activity: Pull ten comments you wrote on recent scripts.

phases.name: Reflective observation
phases.activity: Reflect: what would a student actually do after reading each comment?

phases.name: Abstract conceptualisation
phases.activity: Learn the 'where am I going / how am I doing / where next' feedback model.

phases.name: Active experimentation
phases.activity: Rewrite your ten comments and share three with a student to test them.

andragogy.modules.title: Reading your class outcome heatmap
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: Periodic Test 2 results are now available per outcome. Which three outcomes need remediation in your section?
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A one-page remediation brief for your section.

phases.name: Concrete experience
phases.activity: Open your section heatmap and list surprises.

phases.name: Reflective observation
phases.activity: Reflect on why those outcomes are weak.

phases.name: Abstract conceptualisation
phases.activity: Learn a simple remediation planning framework.

phases.name: Active experimentation
phases.activity: Draft the remediation brief.

andragogy.modules.title: Remediation sprint design
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: Two weeks, one weak outcome, one group of students.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A two-week remediation sprint with checkpoints.

phases.name: Meet the problem
phases.activity: Pick the group and outcome.

phases.name: Identify learning gaps
phases.activity: Identify gaps in your toolkit.

andragogy.modules.title: Clean and summarise my sales MIS
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: The weekly sales MIS takes four hours to clean every Monday. Duplicate dealer names and mixed date formats are the main culprits.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A cleaned, pivot-ready version of the MIS with a reusable cleaning checklist.

phases.name: Meet the problem
phases.activity: Open last month's raw MIS export and list everything that makes it hard to summarise.

phases.name: Identify learning gaps
phases.activity: Write down what I need to learn: TRIM/CLEAN, XLOOKUP, date parsing, pivot tables.

phases.name: Self-directed study
phases.activity: Work through the messy-sales-sheet project.

phases.name: Apply & solve
phases.activity: Clean my own MIS and build the regional pivot.

phases.name: Reflect
phases.activity: Note what took longest and what I can automate next.

andragogy.modules.title: Which average tells the truth? Descriptive statistics
andragogy.modules.realWorldContext: The regional head quotes 'average order value' every review. One dealer's bulk order skews it every month.
andragogy.modules.deliverable: A one-page summary of the dealer data using mean, median, spread and outliers, with a recommendation for which metric to report.

phases.name: Concrete experience

phases.activity: Watch the Walnut LMS video on opportunity cost and marginal thinking (25 minutes) and note one decision from your own work where you ignored an opportunity cost.

andragogy.modules.title: Demand and elasticity: pricing a festive gift box

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What would you do differently if you started this problem again — and why?
andragogy.reflections.text: I started coding the doubly linked list before the singly one worked, and spent two days on segmentation faults. Next time I'll get the simplest version passing tests first. Drawing the pointers on paper before each move operation finally made it click.

feedback.text: Great insight, Rohan — 'simplest version first' is exactly how professional engineers work. Try the same approach for BST deletion: handle the leaf case, then one child, then two children.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What did class time clarify that the pre-work did not? What will you practise next?
andragogy.reflections.text: Unary minus broke my evaluator in class. I understand precedence now but I'm still slow at tracing by hand. I am behind on the module because of the DBMS assignment — I'll finish the deque undo/redo this weekend.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: Describe what you observed during the experience. What surprised you, and why do you think it happened?
andragogy.reflections.text: Sequential inserts made a tree of height 499 — basically a linked list. Lookups were 40x slower than the shuffled run. I had memorised that BSTs are O(log n) without realising that's only the average case.

feedback.text: Exactly the 'aha' this module is designed for. Would you run a 20-minute peer session on rotations for the batch?

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What would you do differently if you started this problem again — and why?
andragogy.reflections.text: We over-engineered the first version with Floyd–Warshall before checking that the transport office only needed single-source routes. Talking to the 'client' earlier would have saved a week.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What did class time clarify that the pre-work did not? What will you practise next?
andragogy.reflections.text: Peer instruction helped — my partner showed me why we pop until a lower-precedence operator appears. I'll practise 10 more conversions.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What do you already know that helps here, and what do you need to find out?
andragogy.reflections.text: I know arrays well but pointers confuse me. I need to understand how a node 'knows' the next one and how to avoid losing the list when deleting.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What principle will you take from this case into your own classroom or work?
andragogy.reflections.text: A competency-based question puts the concept in an unfamiliar context and asks students to decide which mathematics to use. My PT-2 quadratic questions only tested whether students could apply the formula. I rewrote the 'area of a park' question as a case with three sub-parts.

feedback.text: Excellent rewrite, Priya. Please share the park question with the department — it is a good model for the Half-Yearly paper. Watch the reading load for weaker students.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: Describe what you observed during the experience. What surprised you, and why do you think it happened?
andragogy.reflections.text: Anil and I differed by 2 marks out of 5 on the same script. I was rewarding the final answer; he was rewarding correct setting-up of the equation. Without a written scheme both of us were 'right'.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What did class time clarify that the pre-work did not? What will you practise next?
andragogy.reflections.text: Micro-teaching showed I answer my own questions too quickly. With 5 seconds of wait time, 10-B gave far better reasons for why the image is virtual.

feedback.text: Wait time is a small change with a big payoff. Try logging it in one lesson per week.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What position do you take on the case, and what evidence supports it?
andragogy.reflections.text: I think the English paper already has competency in the writing section but not in reading. I want to replace two factual questions with inference-based ones.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What would you do differently if you started this problem again — and why?
andragogy.reflections.text: I would have built the cleaning checklist first instead of fixing errors as I found them. Power Query could do most of this — worth exploring later.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: Describe what you observed during the experience. What surprised you, and why do you think it happened?
andragogy.reflections.text: Removing one bulk dealer moved the West region's average order value by 31%. The median barely moved. We have been celebrating an outlier for three quarters.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What did class time clarify that the pre-work did not? What will you practise next?
andragogy.reflections.text: I always look at the average cost of a carton. The live session showed that for an extra order only the extra cost matters. We turned down a bulk order last month that we should have accepted.

feedback.text: A good example from your own work, Aman. Bring the same thinking to elasticity: what happens to revenue, not just to price.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What do you already know that helps here, and what do you need to find out?
andragogy.reflections.text: I know from the market that customers switch brands when prices go up, but I cannot calculate elasticity confidently, and I mix up cross elasticity with income elasticity. I have fallen behind because of month-end targets.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: What principle will you take from this case into your own classroom or work?
andragogy.reflections.text: A method is only as good as the data behind it. The chikankari shop has five years of offline sales, but online buyers are different people. At work we forecast a new client's tickets from an old client's history, which is the same mistake.

feedback.text: Exactly right, Shreya. Would you lead a short peer session on forecasting for your study group before the re-test?

andragogy.reflections.prompt: Describe what you observed during the experience. What surprised you, and why do you think it happened?
andragogy.reflections.text: I did not expect forfeited shares to create a capital reserve. In my father's shop there is nothing like share capital, so the idea that the company gains from an unpaid call was new.

feedback.text: Good observation, Ankit. Practise the reissue entries twice more; they come up in every sessional test.

andragogy.reflections.prompt: Describe what you observed during the experience. What surprised you, and why do you think it happened?
andragogy.reflections.text: In my first attempt I put the term loan instalment due this year under non-current liabilities. Classifying every item before writing figures fixed most of my errors.

pedagogy.lessons.title: Solving quadratics by factorisation

phases.name: I do
phases.activity: Write x² + 7x + 12 = 0 on the board. Think aloud: check it is in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, list factor pairs of ac = 12 that add to b = 7 (3 and 4), split the middle term, group and take common factors to get (x + 3)(x + 4) = 0, then apply the zero-product rule. Highlight the common error of forgetting to set each bracket to zero.

phases.name: We do
phases.activity: Solve 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0 and 6x² − x − 2 = 0 together on mini-whiteboards. Students call out the product ac and the factor pair at each step; the teacher records the 'split' on the board. Cold-call three students to verify the roots by substitution.

phases.name: You do together
phases.activity: Pairs work through questions 1–8 of the Factorisation Drill. Partner A splits the middle term, Partner B groups and factorises; swap roles every question. Early finishers attempt the NCERT Exercise 4.2 Q2 word problem (product of two consecutive integers is 306).

phases.name: You do alone
phases.activity: Exit ticket (3 questions, increasing difficulty): x² − 3x − 10 = 0; 3x² − 2√6x + 2 = 0; 100x² − 20x + 1 = 0. Students self-mark using the projected answers and mark a confidence level (1–4) beside each.

differentiation.support: Provide a factor-pair table for ac (positive/negative pairs) and colour-coded sign rules. Start with monic quadratics (a = 1) before moving to a ≠ 1.
differentiation.stretch: Factorise quadratics with irrational coefficients (e.g. √2x² + 7x + 5√2 = 0) and explain why some quadratics cannot be factorised over integers.

competencyQuestions: A rectangular mango grove is to be laid out so that its length is twice its breadth and its area is 800 m². Frame the quadratic equation and find the dimensions by factorisation.
Riya says the roots of x² − 5x = 0 are only x = 5 because 'you can divide both sides by x'. Is she correct? Justify your answer.
The product of Sneha's age five years ago and her age ten years later is 16. Represent the situation as a quadratic equation and solve it.
pedagogy.lessons.materials: Mini-whiteboards and markers, NCERT Class 10 Mathematics textbook (Chapter 4), printed exit tickets, Factorisation Drill worksheet

pedagogy.lessons.title: Nature of roots with the discriminant

phases.name: Engage
phases.activity: Show three parabolas on the projector: one crossing the x-axis twice, one touching it, one floating above it. Ask: 'How many solutions does each equation have — and can we tell without drawing the graph?'

phases.name: Explore
phases.activity: In groups of four, use the Discriminant Lab to change a, b and c and record b² − 4ac alongside the number of x-intercepts for six equations in a table. Groups write a conjecture linking the sign of b² − 4ac to the roots.

phases.name: Explain
phases.activity: Derive the quadratic formula by completing the square on ax² + bx + c = 0. Formalise: D > 0 two distinct real roots, D = 0 two equal real roots, D < 0 no real roots. Work through NCERT Example 16 together.

phases.name: Elaborate
phases.activity: Solve: 'Find k so that kx(x − 2) + 6 = 0 has two equal roots.' Then a real-life case: Is it possible to design a rectangular park of perimeter 80 m and area 400 m²? Use the discriminant to decide.

phases.name: Evaluate
phases.activity: Four-question hinge quiz on mini-whiteboards: state the nature of roots for 2x² − 3x + 5 = 0, 3x² − 4√3x + 4 = 0, 2x² − 6x + 3 = 0, and find k for equal roots of 2x² + kx + 3 = 0.

differentiation.support: Give a partially filled table for the Explore phase and a D-sign flowchart card. Pair with a peer tutor (Aarav/Ananya) during Elaborate.
differentiation.stretch: Prove that the equation (a² + b²)x² + 2(ac + bd)x + (c² + d²) = 0 has no real roots unless ad = bc.

competencyQuestions: A ball is thrown so that its height h = −5t² + 20t + 1. Using the discriminant, decide whether the ball ever reaches a height of 25 m.
Aditya claims every quadratic equation has two roots. Use the discriminant to give a counter-example and explain.
pedagogy.lessons.materials: Projector with graphing tool, Discriminant Lab (interactive), mini-whiteboards, NCERT textbook

pedagogy.lessons.title: AP in real life: savings, seats and stairs

phases.name: Experience
phases.activity: Piggy-bank challenge: each group gets a 'savings card' — Ravi saves ₹50 in week 1 and ₹10 more each week. Groups use counters to model the first 6 weeks and predict the amount saved in week 20 without counting.

phases.name: Reflect
phases.activity: Groups share predictions and methods. Prompt: 'What stayed the same each week? Could you jump straight to week 20?' Record the language of 'first term' and 'common difference' as it emerges.

phases.name: Connect
phases.activity: Formalise aₙ = a + (n − 1)d and Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n − 1)d] using the video. Connect to the auditorium seat rows in our school hall (20 seats in row 1, 2 more each row) and to Gauss's story.

phases.name: Apply
phases.activity: Solve the CBSE case-based question set 'AP in Daily Life' in pairs: staircase bricks, a ladder with tapering rungs, and a monthly loan instalment. Each pair presents one solution with justification.

differentiation.support: Provide a term-table scaffold (n, aₙ) and allow use of counters through the Apply phase.
differentiation.stretch: Find how many terms of 54, 51, 48, … must be taken so that their sum is 513, and explain the double answer.

competencyQuestions: Your school auditorium has 20 seats in the first row and each row has 2 more seats than the one in front. If there are 25 rows, how many students can be seated for the Annual Day?

pedagogy.lessons.title: Trigonometric ratios through shadows

phases.name: Engage
phases.activity: Show a photo of the school flagpole and its shadow at 10 a.m. Ask: 'How could we find the height of the flagpole without climbing it?' Collect ideas on sticky notes.

phases.name: Explore
phases.activity: Groups draw three similar right triangles with a 30° angle (different sizes) and measure the sides. They compute opposite/hypotenuse, adjacent/hypotenuse and opposite/adjacent and notice the ratios stay constant.

phases.name: Explain
phases.activity: Name the ratios sin, cos, tan and their reciprocals. Use the video to build the standard-angle table for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° with the 'hand trick'. Students copy the table into their notebooks.

phases.name: Elaborate
phases.activity: Given sin A = 3/5, find the other ratios by drawing the triangle. Evaluate expressions like 2tan²45° + cos²30° − sin²60° in pairs, explaining each step to the partner.

phases.name: Evaluate
phases.activity: Exit ticket: three quick items — define tan θ, evaluate sin 60° cos 30° + sin 30° cos 60°, and find cos A if tan A = 4/3.

differentiation.support: Provide a labelled right-triangle template (opposite / adjacent / hypotenuse) and the standard-angle table as a bookmark.
differentiation.stretch: Prove that the value of sin θ or cos θ never exceeds 1, using the triangle definition.

competencyQuestions: A 1.5 m tall student's shadow is 1.5√3 m long. Find the angle of elevation of the Sun and explain your reasoning.
Diya says sin 30° + sin 60° = sin 90°. Check her claim using the standard values and explain the error.

pedagogy.lessons.title: Ohm's law investigation

phases.name: Engage
phases.activity: Demonstrate a torch that is dim with one cell and bright with two. Ask: 'What changed, and what stayed the same?' Students write a one-line prediction.

phases.name: Explore
phases.activity: Lab activity (NCERT Activity 11.4): groups connect a nichrome wire, ammeter, voltmeter and 1–4 cells in series. Record V and I for each setting and plot V against I on graph paper.

phases.name: Explain
phases.activity: From the straight-line graph, state Ohm's law V = IR and define resistance and its SI unit. Watch the video segment on series and parallel combinations; derive Rₛ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ and 1/Rₚ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃.

phases.name: Elaborate
phases.activity: Real-life wiring: why are household appliances connected in parallel? Solve two numericals — three resistors of 5 Ω, 10 Ω and 30 Ω in parallel across 12 V; and an electric lamp of 20 Ω with a conductor of 4 Ω in series.

phases.name: Evaluate
phases.activity: Five-item exit quiz: identify the graph of an ohmic conductor, compute R from V and I, and choose the combination giving the least resistance.

differentiation.support: Provide a pre-drawn circuit diagram and a V–I table with units. Allow calculator use for the numericals.
differentiation.stretch: Explain why the V–I graph of a filament bulb is not a straight line and what that says about temperature and resistance.

competencyQuestions: An electrician has three 6 Ω resistors. Show how they can be combined to get a resistance of 9 Ω and 4 Ω.

pedagogy.lessons.title: Balancing chemical equations

phases.name: I do
phases.activity: Burn a magnesium ribbon (demo, with safety goggles). Write the word equation, then the skeletal equation Mg + O₂ → MgO. Think aloud the hit-and-trial method: count atoms on each side, balance the element that appears in fewest compounds first.

phases.name: We do
phases.activity: Balance Fe + H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + H₂ together, using an atom-count table on the board. Add state symbols (s), (l), (g), (aq) and conditions over the arrow.

phases.name: You do together
phases.activity: Card-sort in pairs: match 8 reactions to their type (combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, redox) and balance each one.

phases.name: You do alone
phases.activity: Independent practice: NCERT in-text questions page 6 and Exercise Q3. Self-check with the answer key and circle any equation that needed more than three attempts.

differentiation.support: Use molecular model kits / coloured beads to represent atoms while balancing.
differentiation.stretch: Balance redox equations such as MnO₂ + HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + H₂O and identify the oxidising and reducing agents.

competencyQuestions: When a shiny iron nail is dipped in copper sulphate solution, the blue colour fades. Write the balanced equation and name the type of reaction.
Why should a magnesium ribbon be cleaned before burning? Explain using the idea of a protective oxide layer.

phases.name: I do
phases.activity: Divide p(x) = x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1 by (x + 1) using long division, then evaluate p(−1). Think aloud why the remainder equals p(−1) and state the Remainder Theorem.

phases.name: We do

phases.name: You do together
phases.activity: Pairs complete questions 1–10 of the practice set, alternating 'solver' and 'checker'. Checkers must verify with the opposite method (division vs substitution).

phases.name: You do alone

differentiation.stretch: Find a and b if x² + x − 6 is a factor of x³ + ax² + bx − 12, and explain the strategy.

phases.activity: Competency questions: separate camphor from salt, cream from milk, and dyes in black ink. Groups justify the technique and draw labelled diagrams.

differentiation.stretch: Design a flow chart to obtain different gases from air and explain fractional distillation.

competencyQuestions: A farmer's wheat is mixed with husk and small stones. Suggest a sequence of separation methods and give the property each one uses.
